title: Errors in an inventory tool
metaTitle: Errors the floor can fix in one tap
excerpt: When a count fails on the floor, say which item broke and what to do with one hand. A code and a sad illustration waste a person who is holding the box.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, a space where one wrong object is easy to miss if it is not named.
caption: Name the object that does not belong. The floor needs the same courtesy. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the floor see when a scan does not match?
faqs.answer: Say what you expected and what you read, such as expected bin C4 and scanned bin C5, and offer one next action: scan again, or confirm they mean the scanned bin. Keep the count they already typed. A code and a sad illustration do not help someone holding a box under one arm.

faqs.question: What should happen if the network drops mid-count?
faqs.answer: Say whether the last lines are saved on the device. If they are, say they will sync when the connection returns, and let the person keep counting. If they are not, say that plainly and do not pretend the confirm worked. A green success you cannot support becomes a missing pallet later.

faqs.question: Should the floor see the same error as the office?
faqs.answer: The floor needs the item, the bin, and the next tap, while the office may need the sync conflict and the adjustment history. Show each audience its version. A database message on the floor will be ignored, and the count will continue on paper.

markdown:
Inventory tool error states are what the person on the floor reads when a scan, a quantity, or a sync fails. Say what broke and what to do. They are not at a desk. A code and a sad illustration waste the moment, and the box is getting heavy.

The office can have a richer log. The floor needs the item, the bin, and one next tap. If those three are missing, they will finish on paper and enter the "real" numbers later, which is how the tool becomes a second job instead of the job.

## Name the item and the bin

Say which object failed. Bin C4 did not match the scan. The barcode is not in this warehouse. Confirming 12 would take the on-hand count below zero. Those are different problems. "Error" is the same costume for all of them, and it is useless in an aisle.

Include the name printed on the box, not only the internal id. They cannot check an id against a carton without a table. They can check a name and a short code. Put both in the sentence, large enough to read at arm's length, in light that is not your office.

Then the next action, as a big control. Scan again. Enter the code. Mark short. Skip and flag for a lead. One primary action. A second quiet action is allowed if it is a real alternative. A dialog with three equal buttons and a paragraph is a meeting. They cannot hold a meeting and a pallet.

Keep the quantity they typed. A mismatch should not clear the count. Clearing it punishes the careful person and invites a rushed retype that is wrong. If you must discard a value, say you discarded it and why.

The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines describe a standard for content that people can perceive, operate, and understand. On the floor that means the error is text, not a red flash and a buzz alone, and the control is big enough to hit. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the right lens for a message that has to work in glare. Color can support the words. It cannot replace them.

## The failures that actually happen in the aisle

Write sentences for these before you congratulate the team on the happy path.

Wrong bin. They scanned the item in front of them and the task still expects the previous bay. Say both bins. Let them confirm they moved, if the workflow allows, or send them back to the expected bin with that code huge on the screen.

Unknown barcode. Say you do not have that code in this warehouse. Offer type-the-code and flag-for-office. Do not invent a product from a misread. A misread that creates a ghost item is worse than a pause.

Quantity trouble. Negative on-hand, or a count far from the expected number. Ask them to recount before they accept the surprise, and show the expected number beside what they entered. Do not block a true surprise forever. The floor sometimes knows the office is wrong. Give them a way to submit the surprise with a flag, and say the flag is visible to a lead.

Two people counted the same bin. Say the other person's name and the quantity they entered, if your policy allows, and say whose count will stand if they continue. A silent overwrite is how you start arguments the next morning. The error can prevent the argument.

The network dropped. This is normal. Say the last confirmed lines are on the device and will sync, if that is true. Let them keep going. If the device cannot store the line, stop and say so. Do not show a checkmark you have not earned.

The office edited the item while they were counting. Say the name or the expected quantity changed, and show the new values. Ask them to confirm against the box again. A quiet refresh that changes the number under their thumb is how wrong counts get confirmed in good faith.

A short list in the design file keeps this honest:

- Wrong bin, both codes shown, one next scan
- Unknown code, no ghost item, a way to flag
- Surprising quantity, expected value still visible
- Two counters, no silent overwrite
- Offline, a true statement about what is saved
- Item changed mid-count, the new facts shown

If one cannot happen, write that down so a later build does not add a cartoon for it.

## Where the message sits when their hands are full

Put the sentence on the same screen as the item, not in a toast at the top and not in a full-screen takeover that hides the bin code. They need the error and the label in one look so they can compare.

Toasts disappear while they are setting the box down. When they look back, the toast is gone and the line looks unconfirmed. They confirm twice or skip. An inline message stays until they choose the next action.

Sound is a helper. A distinct tone for a bad scan is useful in a noisy aisle only if the visual is also obvious. Some floors ban sound. Some workers wear ear protection. The words have to be sufficient. Haptics too. Nice, and not the message.

Do not use a sad box character. It reads as mockery when the work is physical and the person is behind. Plain language is faster and more respectful. Bin C4 expected. You scanned C5. Scan C4.

A support code can live in small type for the office later. The floor should not have to read it aloud over a radio to be allowed to continue. If a lead must be involved, the primary button can be Call the lead or Flag, and the code can travel with the flag automatically.

## Do not show the office log on the floor

Stack traces, SQL states, and "conflict on row" are office errors. If you show them downstairs, people learn to ignore the screen. Then they miss the one line that mattered.

Give the office a different view of the same event. Who was counting, which bin, what the device stored, whether it synced. That view can be denser. It is used sitting down, with time to repair data. It should still be in sentences at the top, with the raw detail underneath for the person who wants it.

Never let the floor's retry create a second adjustment the office cannot see. If they tap Confirm again after a sync failure, the tool should recognize the same line. Idempotent confirms are a product requirement, not a backend nicety. The error copy can say "Already recorded" if the first tap actually landed.

When the failure is a permission, say the permission. They can count and they cannot write off stock. The button they hit was an adjustment hiding in a count tool. That problem is the next article. In the error itself, "Counts only. A lead has to adjust this bin" is the whole repair. Do not make them guess that a 403 means "ask someone."


## Sync, duplicates, and the morning after

The aisle message is only half the design if the office wakes up to a different number. When a device syncs a line that was confirmed with no network, the floor should not have to do anything. If the sync conflicts, keep the floor's phone quiet unless you need a decision only they can make, such as which physical stack they counted. Do not push a conflict dialog to the device the next morning while they are on a different task. Leave the conflict for the lead's desk, and show the floor a plain status on the count they finished: synced, or still on this device.

If they have already moved on, a banner at the next sign-in can name the bin and say a lead is resolving it. It should not block the new aisle. Blocking today's work because yesterday's sync is unhappy trains people to keep a second notebook. The notebook is the outcome this tool is supposed to retire, and an aggressive dialog is how you invite it back.

The office screen for that same conflict should use the floor's words first. Bin, item name, the two quantities, the two names. The row id can sit underneath for the person who has to repair the ledger. If the office screen leads with the row id, the lead will call the floor and read digits over the radio. You will have moved the error, not resolved it.
## Review it with a box in your hands

Run the wrong-bin scan, the unknown code, and airplane mode, on the device the floor uses, while holding something. You are checking that you can read the bin, hit the next action without a second hand, and still see the quantity you entered.

Ask a floor lead to say what they think happened after one glance. If they say "it errored," the sentence is too vague. If they say "wrong bin, scan C4," you are done with that frame.

Then check the office view of the same event. It should tell the same story in more detail, not a different story. Two stories become a fight about whose count was real.

Permissions are the next place this gets muddled. The next piece is [permissions in an inventory tool](/blog/permissions-in-an-inventory-tool). A control the floor can see and must not use should be explained before it throws, not after they have balanced a carton on a rail to tap it.

If those aisle sentences should be part of the product and not a support macro, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The error is part of the count. Leave it out and the count leaves with it.
